utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case Number IT-98-29-T, the Prosecutor versus Stanislav Galic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Before we resume the examination-in-chief, perhaps it would be wise to turn into closed session for a very short period so in order to find out whether any additional information is available to the Chamber. Yes, private session will do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we turn into open session. It is not confirmed on my screen yet -- yes we are in open session again. Madam Registrar, would you please escort Witness DP1 into the courtroom and may I ask the technicians to take care that during the entry of the witness the facial distortion will be effective.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please be seated. Mr. DP1, may I remind you that you are still bound by the solemn declaration you gave yesterday. I would like to apologise that you had to wait for some time, but we had to deal with procedural issues, meanwhile, the examination-in-chief will be continued by Ms. Pilipovic now. Please proceed, Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Witness answered through interpreter Examined by Ms. Pilipovic: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. DP1.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Today I would merely like to draw your attention to one thing. When you answered our questions, please try to make it short. If you can, try to be concise. I would like to go back to what you said yesterday. It was at 18.22 or 21, and you said that a large number of Serbs had stayed in Sarajevo. Can you tell us why, in your view?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1
utterances.text: I can say with certainty why I stayed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did you stay?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1
utterances.text: I stayed because I was confident that people that I lived with shared all the joys and sorrows. People I worked with were not of the kind to engage in a fight. And secondly, I sincerely believed that the Yugoslav People's Army as a cohesive factor once the whole state to provide sufficient guarantee that no bloody conflict would break out. I must admit that when the Yugoslav People's Army left, I understood once and for all that there could be no coming to terms, that there are two points which hated each other, that they wanted to fight against each other and then I realised I had lost my homeland.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. DP1, you said when you realised that the Yugoslav People's Army left the territory of the city of Sarajevo, that you then realised that you lost your homeland. Why didn't you leave Sarajevo after that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1
utterances.text: I hope you won't hold it against me if I say that perhaps I have some literary bent so I will remind you of Standou's [phoen] words, that one cannot love or should not love two women at the same time. Perhaps that is a question, but it is quite sure that one cannot love two homelands. So one is left with a void. An even if I wanted to leave, I couldn't because the authorities of the day would not allow me and to do something on my own, it would be too risky, because I would have to go across two lines, or rather one front line where the firing never stopped.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like you to explain to us your sentence that the authorities of the day would not let me or did not allow it.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1
utterances.text: Well, the authorities of the day did not allow people to leave. As far as I know it was possible until about late April, and I really wanted from the bottom of my heart to find a way for my child, for my daughter, who was -- who had barely turned 17, and I wanted her to leave the city safely. And even manage to obtain the ticket for the last flight out. I even found a driver who would take her to the plane, but the day one could hear gunfire from a distance, and there was also gunfire in the city and there were barricades, checkpoints all over the place. And the man who came to drive her to the plane, he tried to tell me that there were no -- that it could be done because he ha a badge of the Patriotic League and badge of HOS and badge of Serb forces and that would be sufficient surety, yet I did not dare send her away, and thus I lost all hope that I would be able to leave Sarajevo, not only I, but everybody who was on either side of the front line.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness DP1, you told us that you stopped working, I think you said in August 1992. You said, "I lost my job." Can you tell us whether that principle that people lost their jobs applied to all ethnic groups in Sarajevo or were there some differences?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1
utterances.text: Well, of course, there were differences. The control over the city was taken over by the then -- well, monoethnic authority and of course it looked for people it could trust. Crisis Staffs were set up in Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. early June, a little bit after that, or perhaps before that, I am not quite sure. The house councils were replaced by agents, by building agents and again the criterion was their loyalty to the then-authority, and that is how it went on. As the ruling principle was that those who happened to be on the other side of the front line were fired from their work straight away and those who did not get to work, they were put on a waiting list, and those who did go to work were also under the required labour obligation. But I would say about 95 -- executive personnel -- Muslims -- Bosniaks, then Muslims, accounted for about 95 per cent of the executive personnel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So could you tell us if one of the reasons you lost your job was because you were a Serb?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1
utterances.text: Through my friends, I tried to find out why I was not selected for the work obligation. And in my company, they all agreed that they ask that I be put on to the list to people who would be under work obligation, but they did not get the approval of the higher body, which higher ranking body it was, I do not know and I was never told. What I do know is that Serbs were completely cleansed from all the bodies which in one way or the other had a part in decision making.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you just told me, told us that you believe that the majority of all Serbs in Sarajevo lost their jobs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1
utterances.text: Except those in mixed marriages.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, this is the second leading question, the first being, sir would you tell us if one of the reasons you lost your job was because you were a Serb. I would be grateful if my learned colleague would refrain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, would you please refrain from leading questions unless, as we all know, the issue is not in dispute and it is merely technically leading to points that really count. Please proceed, Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. DP1, you told us yesterday at 18.52 that you had seen mortars.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us where and when.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1
utterances.text: Well, I don't think that I can remember the date. I mean, I saw a mortar in the street in front of my house mounted on a truck. If you want me to, I can explain the conditions under which I saw it, namely, in my house where my wife and my neighbor, I was sitting writing or reading something in a different part of the apartment. It was late afternoon and they called out to me to come and see how mortar was firing shots. I put my papers together and came, but it had stopped firing, and the truck at that moment switched on the engine and left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you saw that truck?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe the truck? What type, what make is it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1
utterances.text: You know, I was on the third floor. I could only see from above, so I really can't say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you see in which direction the -- in which direction it fired?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1
utterances.text: Well, the way it was turned in the street it could fire frontally towards Trebivic, towards Grbavica, or perhaps the next building. I can't -- I can't really say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say that you -- that when you look through the window of your flat you say that frontally one can fire towards Trebivic, can you explain, what do you see from your flat, specifically? When I say "what do you see," do you see some elevations in the city of Sarajevo and which ones?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1
utterances.text: You can see a large part, almost all of Trebivic, and its slopes down to Mojmilo. On the other side, I can see Kosevo hill, Ciglane locality, and the area stretching towards the whole Kosevo stadium.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you tell us that a part of your flat faces Trebivic, can you tell us if you can see in that direction and did you see shelling?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where could you see it from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1
utterances.text: I could see it partly from the balcony, although that was not advisable. I could even see it from the sixth floor with a friend of mine lived, and at times we would come out to his balcony in late afternoon or in the evening, we could go out to watch. Since we survived and somehow overpowered our fear, because and we stopped fearing everything as we did in the beginning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you be more precise and tell us where and when and in what direction?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1
utterances.text: There was evening fighting which looked like sci-fi or action films when you use light bullets and when they are being fired towards Trebivic or from Trebivic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you say towards Trebivic and from Trebivic. Where from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1
utterances.text: From the city.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "from the city" which part of the city? Could you determine that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1
utterances.text: What I could see when I watched it, the impression, one could see the tracing bullets that it could have been from Marin Dvor towards Trebivic. It could have been from Marin Dvor, it could have been from the railway stations it could have been from a third place. It's difficult to say because I am not really a ballistics expert. But these bullets crossed their paths because they went towards each other.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you also said that you saw other sights. Can you tell us what other sights you saw.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1
utterances.text: Well, I saw a number of them. I saw a strange intensive artillery fire in a part which is called, I believe, Colina Kapa or its neighborhood. And after all, I can't really remember the date, but I think it was in early 1994 right in front of my house near the faculty of stomatology, there were some small buildings where former high executives, and I couldn't understand how not a single of these low buildings were hit by any of these projectiles, but a huge number of them fell. I also watched, though it was a bit further away, but I could see Hrasno being shelled and media said that it was Pero Kosjerica Square but I can't really say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you answered my question about watching the shelling from Colina Kapa, did you have any direct knowledge which army had Colina Kapa?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1
utterances.text: At some point, and I am not sure if it was after the shelling, but at some point I heard on the radio and saw it on television, they were marking the successes of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina when they had expelled the Chetniks from Trebivic, cut off the communication Lukavica-Pale, taken Vidikovac and how oxen were being roasted in accordance with the old tradition. That they had reached Stari Sumar which is a well-known coffee shop in Trebivic but then I heard it also denied by those on Pale, because they had the registration, Srna that is what it was called. It was not sure, that the Serb units held on to their positions and our television showed the [indiscernible] Vidikovac and other things --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Will the witness please speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, could you perhaps adjust the microphone so that -- Ms. Pilipovic, perhaps in order to give you some guidance, I see that some ten lines were filled with an answer to your question whether he had any direct knowledge which army held Colina Kapa and on from the third, fourth line, it became clear to me that the answer could have been perhaps "no" as well. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, I told you already to make your answers -- to answer us, if you know, and if you know, you can say "yes." So I will ask you again. Do you know which army held Colina Kapa?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1
utterances.text: Well, I thought I had answered. One side said one thing, the other side said a different thing. I don't know with certainty which Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. troops were at Colina Kapa.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Witness, you said that you heard people say how that there were mortars in carriages at the railway station and fire was opened from them. You told us that you heard it from somebody. Can you tell us who it was that you heard it from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1
utterances.text: Well, it would take some time to remember the names. But I think it was the story that went around. People who boasted about the successes of their troops, and they spoke about the martial arts, about the martial skills which allowed them to score those victories. I mean, it wasn't something that individuals said here and there, it was simply the view expressed by all people whom you came across.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you just told us that in the media it was written that the BH Army was boasting of its successes, that it had taken the positions of the Republika Srpska Army. Could you tell us if you have any knowledge of how often such operations took place, particularly, in this area. You told us about one. But do you have any knowledge if there were any more of such operations and do you know how many?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1
utterances.text: I can only tell you according to what I heard in the media, what I read in the media, because I was not a participant. I know that in early August, Mr. Siber who was a Deputy Commander of the BH army, publicly announced that the citizens should be patient for a couple of days, and that there would be more successes of the BH Army, and that the Ilidza would also be liberated and that there would be a space liberated for normal life. There were such announcements that came more or less regularly after some successes that were publicised as being successes of the BH Army. I think it was also at that time a little later that Mr. Alija Izetbegovic said that within a month, Sarajevo would have this siege lifted and normal life would continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If it will assist you, if you put the headphones so you don't have to struggle with them. Perhaps you can assist. Yes. I see you are struggling all the time. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you said yesterday, 18.53, that you heard frequent shelling around Kosevo.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1
utterances.text: Yes. There were shellings, there were frequent shellings. I always interpreted these shellings to myself as being a part of some operation that was being conducted. If there was a clash between the two sides or attempt to break through the lines, each side would use what it thought was efficient weapons in this conflict.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, when I asked you, in relation to you saying that you heard frequent shellings around Kosevo, could you please tell us whether it was possible to determine whether you, personally, were able to determine from which direction and for where -- from which directions fire was coming and where to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1
utterances.text: I had the opportunity to hear frequently how shells were going, but I have to admit that I was never able to determine by myself, alone, from where these shells were coming. I think that for an ordinary citizen who is inside a room or perhaps if he is sheltering in a basement or in a flat, it is extremely hard to determine where the shells were coming from. I was never able to determine this, although I was able to see that the hill which goes above Pionirska Dolina, Pioneer Valley - I can't remember what it's called - it used to be shelled, there were shells raining, literally in that valley. But in the night, you could see from that hill, there were explosions coming out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you told us that you were active in an association, that you were an activist of an association. Could you tell us, as such, did you get in to any kind of contact with the authorities, civilian or military authorities?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1
utterances.text: Yes, very briefly, I had official negotiation with the then-mayor, Kresevljakovic and there was a group of Serb patients and old people and in November they were not able to leave the city. So they were stopped from leaving. So in this discussions we tried to get them to be allowed to lave because out of 360, 72 had already died. So, he was very nice. We had these talks. And he asked some institution, director of institution, who was in charge of this, who was Mr. Smajic, he was told to become immediately involved in this. And I also went to a reception at Mr. Alija Izetbegovic because of Bajram. And I did have talks after I entered the humanitarian organisation. I also had talks with other administrators who insisted that other organisations should bring in as much food as possible into Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When I asked you about your contacts with civilian and military authorities, could you tell me what were the military authorities that you were in touch with?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1
utterances.text: Well, sometime either it was June or July, it could be sometime around that, three persons in uniform came to the premises of the humanitarian association, wanted an interview, and the point of the interview was the possibility of bringing in food through the -- into Sarajevo through the voluntary association, humanitarian association, because as they said, some permanent communication lines were cut off. I believe that this was about the conflict between the Muslims and the Croats. And there was some negotiations, but this was a very unrealistic request. And still I asked him, what was the quantity of the food involved, and one of them answered that this was a very large quantity, that it could be a very successful business deal and that it would be very easy to work out because there were 35.000 armed people inside the city and 12.000 policemen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. DP1, when you told us that you were an activist of a humanitarian association, could you tell us where was the humanitarian aid distributed, the humanitarian parcels, and how frequently?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1
utterances.text: Well, the humanitarian aid in this association was being given out extremely rarely, distributed extremely rarely. It was humanitarian association that was called the humanitarian association of the aggressor. So nobody wanted to cooperate with us. But this humanitarian association distributed the letters which arrived through the Red Cross, and collected the letters, those people who left Sarajevo, and then we passed them on. And there was a large number of family parcels. And for a year and a month that I was a member of this association, I think that over 155.000 family parcels arrived in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us go back to what you said that you were called "humanitarian association of the aggressor." I just wanted to ask you, in which location were these parcels distributed? Was there a usual place where humanitarian aids were distributed, the parcels?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1
utterances.text: Yes, in several locations of the city. One of the locations was the scout's centre, and then the second one was in Novo Sarajevo. I can't tell you the exact location. One of them is in Stari Grad or in the Old Town in Vladicin Han. So there were several locations for distributions and it was distributed from a centre which was near those places and that is where it was distributed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you listed these places where distribution was done could you tell us for the period from the end of 1992, 1993, 1994, did it happen that during the distribution of humanitarian help, humanitarian aid, there was shooting that occurred, was there firing at the people who came to collect the aid at these locations? Was there ever any firing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1
utterances.text: Yes, once. I think that this happened the middle or end of April. I can't tell you the exact date. But I know it was Orthodox Easter, the time of Orthodox Easter, when people were expecting distribution of eggs which never arrived. Two shells landed on the roof of the scout centre. There were no casualties, nobody died. And I found out from the Croatian Defence Council soldiers who were in this facility, that they had helped 12 people who were slightly wounded because people were probably, most probably wounded by shrapnel. And I remember an interesting sarcastic question asked by a Croatian soldier. He said: "Sir, do you know whether they are firing at us or at you?" At that time I understood that sarcasm as comment on the fact that there were fierce Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. conflicts between the Muslims and the Croats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. DP1, until 18th of July 1991, you lived in Sarajevo, could you tell us, what was the everyday life of your family in Sarajevo? Could you tell us about electricity, gas and water?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1
utterances.text: It was hard. There were periods when there was water, when there was electricity for ordinary citizens, and there were very long periods where there weren't any. But certain, people who had privileges as a rule had both. Once I bitterly observed to a friend that in the evening it was easy to spot who was the new commanders, new authorities, new leaders, because they were able to get electricity and there was gas. So they were able to transform that into electricity. At one point, there was electricity in the entire building, and I was the only one without. But what I want to say is that one occasion, it was early November in 1993, and I spoke to Mr. Hasan Muratovic at the airport, this was with the Serbian side Mr. Koljevic, who was on the Serbian side, and I realised that less hatred between these two would have ensured more water and electricity for Sarajevo because they did discuss the repairs that were supposed to be done to the electrical equipment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I believe that you said there was always gas?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1
utterances.text: Yes, almost always.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any knowledge about the causes of electricity and water shortage?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1
utterances.text: I can only say with certainty what I heard, which was at this discussion, these talks that the electrical equipment was that was damaged, and because they went on the confrontation line and Mr. Muratovic and Mr. Koljevic agreed that the commanders are to be given orders that they should not fire at the workmen who come to repair. This was official, but I heard, and not more than once that this was used as manipulation that the supply of water, supply of electricity was being manipulated with. Because there was a general desire, general belief, general expectation, that only difficult atmosphere, difficult situation in Sarajevo would speed up an intervention from outside and it would lift the siege of Sarajevo, as they said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, if I tell you that on the 3rd and 4th of December 2001, a witness appeared before this Chamber who replying in relation to -- relation to water and electricity, page 678 asking about the water and who had the control of the water. He replied that water supply was under the control of Republika Srpska. Now, could you tell us if this is an exact accurate answer to a question?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1
utterances.text: As far as I know the main two points for water supply, one was Mojmilo and the other one -- the other one was sources and pumps in Ilidza. I was not there. I don't know exactly where the line went. But if this belonged to Ilidza, then it was probably was under the control of the Republika Srpska. But and also so the pumps, even the Serbian pumps couldn't work without electricity, so obviously it was all linked.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us if the other one was under the -- other one was in Mojmilo. Can you tell us under whose control Mojmilo was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1
utterances.text: I found out after I left Sarajevo the second time because during the war, I left Sarajevo four times, or I got out of Sarajevo four times, and then I was informed, and I saw that Mojmilo was under the control of the BH Army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. DP1, you told us that you got out of Sarajevo four times. Could you tell us how easy was it for citizens of Sarajevo to leave it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1
utterances.text: From the moment that the conflict broke out, no citizens in Sarajevo could leave easily. I managed to get out because I was a humanitarian worker and I managed to get all the permissions from police, army, and so on. The first time I left was in April 1993, and I got out. I was out for one hour in Ilidza. That time I then slightly adjusted my opinion about the conflict. I was amazed that Ilidza was severely damaged, that it was much more damaged than the part of town that I was. And on the demarcation line so from Stupska Petlja,, the street which goes from the main road towards Ilidza, I can't remember it exactly, this was an actual wasteland. There was nothing that could be seen. This was all destroyed. So I got out when I was allowed, and on the agreement of the other side, that is, the Serbian side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. DP, you told us that you left the city, and that you were in Ilidza. Could you tell us the demarcation lines that you spoke about, and which were, as you say, ethnic lines, could you tell us what was the percentage of the urban part of Sarajevo that was under the control of one side and how much under the control of the other side? Or perhaps you could tell us according to municipalities, which part of the town was under the control of one side, and which was under the control of the other?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1
utterances.text: I am not quite clear with the expression "urban part of town," because urban part of town is also Ilidza, urban part of town is also Ilijas. These were all parts of the city because they were connected with public transport, with infrastructure. So in my opinion, all of these were urban parts of town. But, according to what I saw when I got out, this demarcation line ran approximately, according to the lines which on both sides represented the majority population, so the demarcation lines from Grbavica, they followed the street where there was more majority Serb population. The other side majority Muslim and so on. Grbavica was a majority Serbian. Stari Grad, Old Town, majority Muslim and so on. So I felt that these lines were like ethnic demarcation lines dividing the city under the control of two strong nationalist groups that were in the city. When I finally left Sarajevo and I left Sarajevo on several occasions, when I finally left Sarajevo, I found exactly the very same demarcation lines in place the first time and the last time I left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. DP, you told us about the discussion with civilian authorities that you had when a convoy of six Serbs was supposed to leave Sarajevo. Could you tell us, bearing in mind the activities that you were involved in and the possibility of contacts with authorities, could you tell us about the position, situation of Serbs in Sarajevo, and did this convoy ever leave Sarajevo with the six Serbs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1
utterances.text: I think that was 9, 10, 11th in 1992. I was involved directly. At the time I did not belong to a single association, not even humanitarian. But I was interested because one of the people who were ill was my grandmother. So incredible things happened the way I felt -- the way I saw them, that they, in the morning, the convoy was supposed to leave of 900 or 1.000 people --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, could you please tell us briefly whether this convoy left or not.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1
utterances.text: I think only three buses left. I think the others didn't. All the sick people didn't leave including those that were in the wheelchairs and stretchers and that was a cold November day. Only three buses left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, during my examination you told us that there were days with no electricity and no water, and there were also situations that only you in the entire building had no electricity, that is, water. Now, could you tell us, where did your family get water from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1
utterances.text: In different locations because occasionally there would be some water, and then we would fill up canisters, and then occasionally, very rarely in the beginning, there were cisterns, tanks that came. And then we went to Bistrik because there was a brewery there which had a lot of water and people would wait in the line to get water. But I never want to those -- I never went to the brewery because there was this belief that Caco was there, that he was without mercy, that he was arresting people, so I didn't dare go. That was one reason I didn't go. And the second reason was for a while I was injured and I had broken a rib so I was not able to go to Bistrik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. DP, you told us at that part of Bistrik there was Caco and that he was arresting people. Could you tell us which people he was arresting and why and do you have any knowledge of this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1
utterances.text: Well, arrests of people in the street started rather early, sometime in May because of digging of trenches. The second wave started Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. in June after the mobilisation was proclaimed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I can see that I rise to my feet a little late. The question asked by my learned colleague was in part: "You told us at that part of Bistrik there was Caco and that he was arresting people." When one looks at the previous answer of the witness, he in fact said "I never went to the brewery because there was this belief that Caco was there." My objection is to the question on the basis of that it doesn't accurately state the evidence, and I think that is in important in respect that the question should do that, Mr. President. In other words, that it was a "belief" and not a "fact."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, in the English translation it says that it was "believed" that Caco was there and was arresting people. So therefore it would have been appropriate to see what is the basis of this belief or assumption or what the knowledge of the witness exactly is. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. That would have been my question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who did you get this information from? So, did you see this, did you hear this? If you heard it, who did you hear it from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1
utterances.text: I heard it from Mr. Rade Savic which was a long time friend and who spent nine months digging trenches in Trebivic and the surrounding area. And I know also before the war and also another friend of mine, Radivojevic, also went to dig trenches. This is common knowledge, that in Sarajevo it was normal, it was usual for people in the first months of war, people who were not in the army, who do not have a work obligation, they would be just gathered in the street, rounded up, and they would be taken to dig trenches.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, looking at the clock, if you could find a suitable moment for a break, relatively soon, that would be appreciated.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. We will have a break. I just wanted to confirm, to have it confirmed by the witness --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So for these people whose names you quoted, from them you heard that it was Caco, and Caco's unit, they were the ones who were arresting people and taking them to dig trenches.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I heard that. And I was the prey of such arrests.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I believe that this is the time for us to have a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We will adjourn until quarter past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. DP, yesterday during the examination you identified for us a number of buildings in your area where the troops were accommodated. Can you tell us if you personally saw -- during the time which you lived in Sarajevo -- did you see those buildings shelled? And please say yes or no.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. You say, "yes." Can you tell us when?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1
utterances.text: I can tell you about one occasion and I already mentioned it. It was the scout's home which accommodated a Croat unit. So shells frequently fell there. And as you walked by, you could see marks. And I already said that next to the faculty of stomatology of dentistry, there were -- one could see a large number of projectiles which had fallen around small buildings in a park around the between them. I do not know whether the shells hit Skerliceva. One hit the building next to mine. Another one hit my building or rather in my -- and that was in the immediately vicinity of those buildings. So the answer could be yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. DP, when you mentioned the faculty of stomatology, can you

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, if I would have a map with some places on it, and someone would say it is 1.000 metres, then you have a lot of other places that were at the distance of 1.000 metres, but the closer comes, the more identifiable it is. You asked for the protective measures. The Chamber granted them. I will ask the Registrar to make a redaction on from page 33 -- no my pages are -- or I hope they are correct. Page 33, line 8. And would you please take care that the protective measures you sought really remain effective.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. With your leave, I would like to show the witness a map, and then would ask that we go into a closed session, and then he could mark it and if he can help us by telling us which part of the city it is, so that he explains to everybody what he has explained, what he has answered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It is up to you to use your time as you deem it good. On the other hand, you might be aware that if it is about the general geography of the city, the Chamber has become more and more familiar with it already. So if it is just about the area, the region, it might be repetitious, but if it goes into more detail, please proceed. Yes, we will then --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will then turn into closed session so that whatever is on the ELMO -- Ms. Pilipovic, if we do not use the ELMO, I don't know whether the witness has to point at several locations, because that can only be done through the ELMO. If it's just a matter of explaining it could be done in private session as well. But if you think the ELMO would be of any use, then we should go into closed session.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we need the ELMO after all. Of course, I can first ask the witness if whether he can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are in closed session now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are in open session again. Please proceed, Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. DP, you marked the Kosevo Hospital, and I think you said that you visited it four times while you were in Sarajevo; is that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1
utterances.text: Three times. Three times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Can you tell us, on those three occasions when you went to the hospital, did you next to the hospital or in the hospital see any armed men?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1
utterances.text: I went there -- the first time, I went there to see Dr. Starovic, whom I had known for many years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you don't have to go into all this explanations. Just tell us if you were there and what --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1
utterances.text: Yes. There were quite a number of soldiers at the entrance into the hospital and some of them were armed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us when was that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1
utterances.text: I think it was sometime in the autumn of 1992, because Dr. Starovic was wounded by a sniper while he was in his yard. He was receiving their treatment and so we went to pay him a visit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, I would like to ask you for your protection, not to give us any names, not to mention names of people. And I am asking you about the second and third time when you went there. When was that and did you see armed men there, too, on those occasions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1
utterances.text: I went to the orthopaedic clinic because I had some problems with my arm, and there was a war commander, war director, Dr. Cibo [phoen] and from the window of the surgery of the doctor that I went to see, he said that there was a group of his armed escorts who were in uniform and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, again it seems to be another case of the witness relating what someone else has told him was the case as we heard yesterday in relation to the Military Hospital. I appreciate that hearsay is admissible and it is a question of weight. But if it is entirely dependent upon what he was told by someone else, in my respectful submission, it is of no assistance to the Trial Chamber. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As I indicated yesterday, it is to some extent left to the parties to draw a line between what is useful hearsay and what is hearsay that would finally not assist the Chamber. Ms. Pilipovic, it is also a matter of how you use your time and of course, direct knowledge of witnesses might be to be preferred. So I -- the Chamber is aware that you cannot always forecast what the answer of the witness will be, but please keep that in mind.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, when you told us that you went to the clinic for the second time and you mentioned a certain commander, a doctor, did you personally see at that time when you were there, did you see armed men?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1
utterances.text: I went to see Dr. Remzo Bajrovic who was an orthopaedic surgeon, and through the window it could be seen that a group of soldiers were passing by. He then told me that this was the new director of the centre for orthopaedic surgery that was Dr. Cibo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. DP1, could you tell us this third time when you say that you went, when was that? When did you go to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1
utterances.text: I had some heart problems and I --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you just please be precise, when that was and did you see armed men, armed soldiers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1
utterances.text: I did not see armed soldiers at the time because I went to see Dr. Lipa who was a -- before that, he was a health minister.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1
utterances.text: You are welcome.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you went to the hospital on these occasions, did you, on the way from your house to the hospital, did you observe or rather did you see any weapons and armed men?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1
utterances.text: Yes, I had to go past the aforementioned locations where I specified that there were soldiers, and in those locations I saw the soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see any weapons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During your stay there, your stay in Sarajevo, did you see armed men in movement or movement of these units?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1
utterances.text: On several occasions, I saw large groups of soldiers for whom I assumed, I presumed, according to their appearance, that they were returning from the front line.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. DP, in the building where you lived, were there troops there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1
utterances.text: In the building where I lived, occasionally, on two or three occasions, there would be some wild unit that came in to premises that belonged to a company which had just ceased to function. I think it was a company from Croatia or from Serbia. But occasionally, a group of 30 men would appear there and be there for 7 or 8 days and the story was they were called a "wild unit or an irregular unit."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. DP, could you tell us if in the part of town where you lived, were there facilities that were shelled?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1
utterances.text: The shells were falling around the faculty of medicine and around the faculty of stomatology. I already said that the shells were falling in this mini-locality next to the stomatology faculty. There was also shells falling in the Skerliceva street where I --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, you already said that. Do you have any knowledge about other parts of town, did you see facilities that were shelled?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1
utterances.text: Yes, I saw shelling of the former government of Bosnia-Herzegovina, government building. I saw shelling of facilities in Marin Dvor, the so-called Unisys skyscraper, in that part of town, I mostly saw those high-rise buildings were shelled and were targeted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you tell us that you saw that high-rise buildings were shelled, did you have any knowledge whether in those buildings there were troops in there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1
utterances.text: I never went to any of those buildings. Although this is not an argument, I have to say, that talks, the rumours had it, that from the top of those buildings, snipers were active, although I never saw any snipers, because I never went past there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. DP, could you tell us --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I make the same objection. But I appreciate what the ruling is likely to be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The question was whether the witness had any knowledge and I think when the answer was given Ms. Pilipovic intended to put the next question, so I can't prevent the witness to give the answers Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. he has in mind. And I would not prevent him from doing so. But perhaps, in general, Mr. DP1, and I repeat what I said yesterday to you, the most important is what you observed by yourself. And sometimes it might be of specific importance to know what someone told you. But, in general, I would not say for certain but in general what rumours that were there is not of much assistance for this Chamber, since we do not know the sources of these rumours. So unless there is a specific reason to refer to that, I invite you to answer the questions of Ms. Pilipovic in such a way that we get clear information about what you experienced, what you observed, and only if really necessary also what general information that was there, and then preferably, with a specific source of your information. Please proceed, Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. DP, could you tell us on the basis of what information did you tell us, and who did you hear from that there was snipers on those high-rise buildings?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1
utterances.text: On the basis of a general opinion there was a front, there were a front line, there were two parties on two opposing sides, and they were trying to eliminate each other with the use of weapons. And I can say that I heard some stories, I heard stories about snipers in my own building. There were snipers, and this is not contested. There was firing all over the place. And I am just saying that the general opinion that people held is that this was the way that was used to eliminate firing positions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. DP. Mr. DP, on several occasions you mentioned that you watched television, and that you listened to the radio. Could you perhaps tell us what was media -- what were media reports like? Did they faithfully report about what was happening in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1
utterances.text: I have to say that truth is the first casualty of war, and then morality. The warring parties used the media as a type of psychological war, and really, you could not believe the media at all because they were just expressing the opinions of the parties in power. They were instigating in people, they were spreading hatred, that is my assessment of the work of the media.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Do you have any personal knowledge, first-hand knowledge, if you do please tell us, on the basis of which information do you know if in the city of Sarajevo there were workshops for manufacturing weapons? If you don't have personal knowledge, please say no.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1
utterances.text: I don't have any personal knowledge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you heard about it, could you tell us where from, who from did you hear about it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1
utterances.text: When shells are flying and when there is fear in corridors and in the basements where we gathered, there were all sorts of stories. And naturally, there were these stories, and also stories that said that new weapons were invented that would eliminate enemy overnight and so on. But of course these are just stories and I wouldn't retell them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. DP. You told us yesterday in the examination-in-chief that there were lots of weapons in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us, did you personally have weapons, and do you have any knowledge how Serbian population was getting the arms in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1
utterances.text: As a former manager, I had a trophy pistol and I had quite a lot of problems to hand it over. And I handed it over or surrendered it, thanks to a friend --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. I would just like you to answer in relation to your knowledge, your personal knowledge, whether you know if a party -- and I am particularly -- there were several parties -- but, did the SDS arm Serbs in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1
utterances.text: I am a Serb. I am a member of the Serb nation, of the Serbian people. I was not armed. I have -- there are seven other families who are related to me of the same surname, they were in Sarajevo as well. And they were not armed. It doesn't mean that they were not doing the arming. Before the war, the weapons were timidly discussed, but when the war started, then suddenly people started talking how people got weapons for themselves, for their children, in order to defend Bosnia-Herzegovina. And then I also drew the conclusion that wherever there is war, there is always a large number of weapons smugglers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. DP, you as an activist of an organisation or an association you said that people who knew about it called it "aggressors organisation." Could you tell us if there were Serb families in Sarajevo in 1993, in that part of town where you lived in, that you say was under the control of the BH Army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1
utterances.text: Together with the group of activists considering that we had a first, quantity of food, we decided to distribute it by getting to every Serb family. And we had a register, we kept a register, and I believe it is accurate, in September 1993, 15.300 Serb families, out of that there were about 15 per cent of mixed families, and then there were some Serbs who were closer to the front lines. They didn't feel like they could say that they were Serb, they refrained from that. And then some of them -- some of the Serbs didn't wish to declare themselves as Serbs. So that this conclusion could be drawn that according to this -- according to this register, there were 1.6 family members. That was the average number for a number of members in Serb families in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During your stay in Sarajevo did you have any unpleasant things that happened to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say, "yes," could you perhaps tell us about these unpleasant things that happened and what form did they take?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1
utterances.text: War is a situation where reason is absent and there are no human laws, but war laws. And I always interpreted this as somebody's need to identify themselves as a member of an elite and in order to do this, somebody else needs to be pushed out of the way. I am not saying to eliminate, but that is the idea. I had some encounters with the police, but I am still here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. DP, during this trial we have heard many witnesses who told us that cemeteries were shelled in Sarajevo. While you were in Sarajevo, do you have any personal knowledge of this and did you ever see this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1
utterances.text: Once on TV I believe that this is Partizanska Groblje, Partisan Cemetery, which is right next to the engineering faculty and because I saw that on TV, I don't know how relevant it is but this counterinformation so to speak which came from the Serbian press agency this was announced that the shell had targeted faculty of engineering which was a centre --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, the objection that I make is similar to the one I made earlier today and another one yesterday. In this sense, that I don't object to the question, I do object to the answer, both yesterday and today, Mr. President, you implied that it was not possible to object to an answer. My respectful submission is that the Trial Chamber is entitled to strike out part of an answer or an answer in its entirety, if it is not admissible evidence. And in this case, the question -- the answer is clearly not responsive to the question. Furthermore it is hearsay of, in my respectful submission, no assistance to the Trial Chamber for this reason: He is recounting what he saw on TV, having only a few minutes ago, made clear his personal view that the media was unreliable as a source of information. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Strike out answers, of course, is mainly functioning in a jury system where it should be clear for a jury what they could take into account and what they could not take into account and the mere fact that the witness saw something on television does not make it in itself inadmissible. But, Ms. Pilipovic, where the witness himself indicates, after he has told this Chamber that the media were an instrument for the party that was controlling the area, perhaps after he has told us that it might not be relevant, perhaps it would have been appropriate for you to see whether it was useful spending of time. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace, I think that the answer confirms what the witness said before, that he saw on TV something, and after that he received the counterinformation.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I must say I read it differently. I read it as meaning that he has only source of information in relation to a particular incident is what he saw on TV. Although, I do note that he refers to some confirmation, so I take your point, Your Honour, to that extent. But both sources are media sources presenting a particular view as to what happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: That is exactly what he said before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please proceed, Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. DP, you mentioned technical faculty or was it engineering?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1
utterances.text: I think it is faculty of engineering.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know if there were troops quartered in the faculty of engineering?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1
utterances.text: If it is about what I saw personally, I haven't seen them, but I did hear about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say that you heard about it, could you tell us where from and when?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1
utterances.text: I said from the media, and I really told you that I did not believe the media in the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us, when we spoke about the facilities, could you tell us whether during the war telephones operated in Sarajevo during the war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1
utterances.text: In the part of Sarajevo where I lived for a while there was no -- there were no telephones that were operating because the central post office was destroyed. But then later on some individuals who were at important positions, they had telephone connection. It wasn't en masse, but they did have them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say, "individuals who were in high positions or carried out a higher or more important functions," could you tell us who were these people and where did they work?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1
utterances.text: I only used telephones in two locations. This was the former postal savings buildings, because I knew the director of the PTT who was the same director as before the war and stayed after the war, and he was -- beginning of the war. And in my own buildings where the neighbours above me, a professor and a lady who worked in the state administration, they had telephones.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. DP you told us that you communicated in the city. What I want to ask you is whether in 1992 you saw people who had had injury or were killed by snipers or as a consequence of shelling in the street, specifically, July, August, September October, 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I saw the incident in Miskin Street. That was at the end of May. And the [indiscernible] conflict in my opinion took place somewhat later in the autumn that year. I personally didn't find dead bodies, except in Vasa Miskin Street.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I may just confer with my co-counsel. With your leave, my co-counsel would like to ask a few questions so that we can be more efficient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, leave is granted.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Examined by Mr. Piletta-Zanin:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Hello. Witness, I would like to ask you some questions and I would like to ask you to answer them as briefly as possible, please. First question: Did you hear -- I am not just saying see -- did you hear that weapons were fired in the area where you lived, and I am talking about heavy weapons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1
utterances.text: Apart from the incident that I have already described, I couldn't -- I wouldn't be able to locate this, and I wouldn't be able to --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, I am not asking you to locate it, but only if you heard it; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Did you hear it often, very often, rarely, relatively often?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1
utterances.text: Well, quite often.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Witness, now I would like us to go back to the question of distribution of humanitarian aid. You told us about this distribution, and what I would like to know whether in your neighborhood, this distribution of aid took place often, rarely, quite often, quite rarely, and so on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1
utterances.text: Humanitarian aid that was distributed by the UNHCR was regular, it was insufficient, however, it was distributed equally to every citizen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am going to interrupt you. When you say "regularly" what was the rhythm? What was the frequently? Was it once a fortnight? Once a month?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1
utterances.text: According to the rule, it was once a month, but it was quite often late.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Witness, do you know if, on top of this distribution, were there specific distributions of water and where, also of bread -- or of bread?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1
utterances.text: I know that there were other humanitarian organisations that used specific channels, specific criteria. They had privileged criteria and privileged channels to distribute humanitarian aid and this did not encompass the whole population. Bread was not distributed or rather it was distributed in certain locations for money. So it was sold, bought and sold for coupons. And these were certain locations where one was supposed to go and wait and then approximately one would get 250 grams per day when there was bread.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Now in relation to these places, can you tell us where they were, those points, the points which everybody knew?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1
utterances.text: Well, more or less, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if these were places which everybody knew, then I think people waited, what, inside or outside, in the street?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I object, Mr. President. I stand to be corrected, but I don't see where the witness said that the places of distribution were places which everybody knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He has just answered. The witness has just said: "More or less, yes," I think that is what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And the question was: "Now in relation to these places, can you tell us where they were, those points, the points which everybody knew?" And given that it is examination-in-chief, that is a leading question which does not appear to reflect the earlier evidence of the witness. It amounts to putting words in the witness's mount, which is the reason for my objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The objection is denied although, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, it might be wise that if the witness said "more or less," that in your next question you will refer to his precise answer. But I may also remind the parties that if no one would know where to get the bread, would that make any sense? I mean, apart from the legal and procedural aspects involved in it, I wonder whether there would be one place in the world where no one would know where to get the bread. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you are right, but I was about to -- thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These places, Witness, where people went were they some indicated queues or perhaps people didn't have the time to wait?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1
utterances.text: You -- one waited and yes, there were queues.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Since there were queues since you tell us in your answer and I would prefer a yes or no, do you know of any example of one of those queues that everyone knew about and that was shelled, that you had seen.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1
utterances.text: Only when I mentioned Vasa Miskin Crni Street.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps we shall come back to this incident later on. But you personally, apart from that incident, are you aware of any other incidents yes or no?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, you spoke a while ago about the engineering faculty. Do you know if it worked during the war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say that it is that you don't know or that it did not work?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1
utterances.text: I said I do not know. That was my answer. I did not know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, your answer was no, that is what came out. Thank you very much. Witness, now I would like to ask you something about possible marketplaces in your area. Were there green markets there? I believe you mentioned a while ago that you talked about in the area that you lived, were there any marketplaces?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1
utterances.text: Well not quite near me. At a certain distance, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that area, was it an open area; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1
utterances.text: Open.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know if this marketplace, to your knowledge, was ever the target of mortar attacks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1
utterances.text: I heard about it, but I did not see it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear about other attacks on other markets or perhaps the area where you lived, resided and lived?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1
utterances.text: Well, I am referring to them. I told you about those places. I told you that I heard -- that I heard -- that I had heard about those markets.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But which markets are you referring to? Could you -- are we talking about something else outside your neighborhood? What do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1
utterances.text: I mean, the Markale market, and the market at Alipasino Polje. The media reported that it had been hit by shells and of course showed those sites on television.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, I would like to make something quite clear: The question that I asked you a moment ago, namely, whether the market in your neighborhood was ever shelled, and you said "yes." But did you mean that market or perhaps some other market?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1
utterances.text: As far as I can remember I said that in my neighborhood, strictly speaking, there was -- there were no markets, that they were at a certain distance. I used to go to three different markets. I went to Markale and Kosevsko brdo, Kosevo hill there at the latter place, there were no shellings there. That I heard and saw on television the shells had hit the Markale market.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right, Witness, do I understand you then correctly, if I understand your testimony, admitting the fact that the market in the area where you lived, to your knowledge was never shelled; is that it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: If I had correctly read the transcript and heard the interpretation, the witness has --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Use the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: As I understand the witness's evidence he has made clear repeatedly that there was not a market in his immediate area. Again the question seems to be incorrectly putting the evidence to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, the objection is sustained.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, apart from the market that you spoke to me about, that is the Markale and the incident that you mentioned, were there, to your knowledge, other cases, are there cases when markets were targeted?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1
utterances.text: Apart from what I already said and those two markets which I mentioned, I did not hear of any others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, I now go back to bread queues, bread lines, that is, queues of people waiting for bread. To your knowledge, were there other places where people also had to queue in the area that you knew, for instance, to queue for water or whatever other need?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1
utterances.text: Except water and bread, I am not aware -- at least I did not have to queue anywhere else. Needless to say, there were queues in front of humanitarian organisations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To your knowledge -- and now I am not talking about markets, I am talking about queues -- are you aware of water queues that were targeted in your area, neighborhood?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1
utterances.text: In my area, that did not happen. But I did hear that once a shell fell --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, no no. I am only asking about your direct knowledge, Witness. So that we avoid any difficulty.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1
utterances.text: In my area, in my neighborhood where we had water from time to time, but at times we had to queue for it and a shell never fell on those water queues.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Is there a mosque or mosques in the area in which you live?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1
utterances.text: Well at a distance of some 300 metres in different directions, there were two mosques.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they destroyed or targeted with a view to destroying them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1
utterances.text: No, while I was there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The minarets, were they in place during the war?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I object, Mr. President, on the basis of relevance as this has come up in the last few weeks, the accused has not been charged in relation to targeting places of worship or other buildings, and therefore, this question and this line of questioning simply lacks relevance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think so, Mr. President. I think if there was a campaign, really, a campaign whose purpose was to cleanse, then I do not see why -- I do not see why -- I mean, this is the war logic. Why should one avoid the symbol which is most painful, which are most representative of a particular group. The Defence is out to prove that these symbols were always protected and that is the best proof that there was no such campaign.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The objection is denied. The circumstances as the Defence intends to demonstrate at this moment might be of some relevance for the - for both the - whether the shelling was at random or not or whether there was a campaign. It could shed some light on that, so the objection is denied. Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. I say "please proceed" but it is time for a break as well. So I don't know whether this would be a --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I think it would be great and we should need only a few minutes after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If there are no more objections.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, there is something I would seek to raise at some appropriate time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: In relation to, I suppose it could be called a housekeeping matter at a time convenient to the court but preferably today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, is it of such urgence or that it could wait until just a couple of minutes just before we adjourn or a couple of minutes before 7.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: That could be fine, Mr. President, and I think I could telegraph my intentions by reminding you of some guidelines that the Prosecution needs reasonably urgently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I am not sure whether I am give you after answer to that. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, you said you needed only a couple of minutes. Is that -- without any objections, you added to that, unnecessarily. If that would be five minutes, I would like to continue so that the cross-examination could start after the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It will be more than five minutes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will then have a break until five minutes to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, these water queues that you spoke to us about, we would like to know if the distribution of water happened frequently or not, was it on a daily basis or not? What can you tell us about it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1
utterances.text: Well water was not distributed practically. Everybody had to go and look for water for himself, on those occasions when there was no water at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. And where did you find yours and were there perhaps some points where you had access to water?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1
utterances.text: Well, such points were in Pionirska Dolina and there was next one next to the brewery and at times near some houses --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, I am going to interrupt you. Don't give us too many details, please. Simply tell us if you were aware of such-and-such locations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1
utterances.text: Yes, one could hear it from one's neighbours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And to your knowledge, Witness, did you ever see such places shelled in your neighborhood?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, I am now moving to another subject. You spoke to us about a "wild unit," remember?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. To begin with, were there some other similar units, units that could be compared to that particular unit, whose members you could meet personally in that part of the city?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there many such units, one, several?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1
utterances.text: Towards the end of April and in early May, there were a number of such units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, those men, how strong were they were these groups, 10? 30? Less?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, perhaps my friend could ask what year with the answer was "towards the end of April, early May," I assume that is 1992, but perhaps that can be clarified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please clarify this.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I shall be happy to do so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, are we talking about 1992, 1993 or what? Which year are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. So I will go back to my question. How strong were those groups, approximately?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1
utterances.text: Those who were in these building now and 10, were at times 10 men strong, at times 20, at times 5. I couldn't really.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, and were those men armed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us what kind of weapons did you see, for instance, were they? I am saying for instance, were they small arms or something that you could wear in your belt or rifles, automatic rifles, machine-guns or I don't know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1
utterances.text: As a rule, those were light weapons. I didn't see any long barrels.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For a technical reason, when you say, "light weapons," Witness, do you include -- are you talking about those weapons which you carry over your shoulder, that is, rifles, or do you mean just small arms?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1
utterances.text: Well, they at times had pistols and Hecklers, and they had knives and automatic ones, too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Witness, I would like to move on to another line of questioning, namely, to the trenches. Did you see in your neighborhoods or when you went further out, did you see any trenches?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, this question is leading on purpose, Mr. President, but I believe that we agree that there were trenches.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
